# p0_1password_account (Resource)

A 1Password account whose items P0 can share, through one of your 1Password connectors. When a request for an item is approved, P0 has the connector create a read-only share link to it that only the requestor's email can open.

The account's service account decides what people can request: P0 lists the vaults the service account can see, and their items, straight from 1Password, so there's no list of vaults to keep in P0. To make a vault requestable, give the service account access to it in 1Password. To stop, remove that access.

P0 never holds the service account token. You store it in your own secret manager, in the connector's cloud, and the connector reads it on every call. This resource tells P0 which connector shares the account's items and where the token's secret is.

**Important:** Create the token, store it and let the connector read it before you apply this resource, in an earlier apply or in the same one with this resource depending on the connector's read grant, as the example does. Creating this resource has P0 validate the install through the connector: the connector reads the secret, signs in to 1Password with the token, checks that the service account can see at least one vault, checks that the account's sharing policy allows sharing an item with a specific person by email, and reads its own allowed domains. It creates no share link. If a check fails, the apply fails with P0's message. IAM changes can take a few seconds to take effect, so if the connector is denied the secret right after it is granted, apply again.

The connector, the secret manager and the secret are fixed when the account is added, so changing `id`, `connector`, `secret_manager` or `token_secret_name` replaces the installation. Changing `one_time_links` or `request_limit` updates the installation in place. To rotate the token, store the new one as a new version of the same secret, which needs no change here. If the account is already added in P0, import it rather than creating it: P0 refuses to add an account twice. An installation that P0 hasn't finished, such as one imported before its checks passed, plans an update, and applying it finishes the install.

**Prerequisites:**

- A 1Password Business or Enterprise account.

- A 1Password connector, installed with `p0_1password_connector`. The token's secret must be in the connector's cloud: AWS Secrets Manager for a connector on AWS Lambda, or Google Secret Manager for one on Cloud Run. It can be in another account or project.

- A 1Password service account for P0, with the permissions **Read Items** and **Share Items** on exactly the vaults people may request, and no other vault. Its token starts with `ops_`. Store the token as a secret in the account and region, or the project, that `secret_manager` names, outside Terraform, which keeps the token out of Terraform's state.

- A sharing policy that lets the account's members share items with a specific person by email, for at least as long as people may request access.

- Read access to that one secret for the connector's identity, the connector's `connector_identity`, and to no other secret. P0 names the secret in each call, so any other secret the connector can read is one a call could point it at.

  On AWS, give the connector's role `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` on `arn:aws:secretsmanager:<secrets_region>:<account_id>:secret:<name>-??????`. Secrets Manager adds a hyphen and six random characters to the name in a secret's ARN, and `??????` matches those, so the grant covers this one secret. If a customer-managed KMS key encrypts the secret, also give the role `kms:Decrypt` on that key, with the condition that `kms:ViaService` is `secretsmanager.<secrets_region>.amazonaws.com`. A secret in an account other than the connector's needs a customer-managed key, because the default `aws/secretsmanager` key can't be used from another account, and in that account the secret's resource policy and the key's policy must allow the connector's role too.

  On Google Cloud, give the connector's service account `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` and `roles/secretmanager.viewer` on the secret itself, not on its project.

- P0's secret manager integration for where the secret is: AWS Secrets Manager (`p0_aws_secrets_manager`) for the AWS account, or Google Secret Manager for the Google Cloud project.

**Note:** This integration is currently in beta.

For the full install steps, see [1Password](https://docs.p0.dev/integrations/resource-integrations/1password).

## Example Usage

```terraform
# Adds the 1Password account that signs in at acme.1password.com, whose
# service account token is in AWS Secrets Manager, in the AWS account of the
# connector on AWS Lambda that the p0_1password_connector example installs.
# For a connector on Cloud Run and a token in Google Secret Manager, see gcp.tf
# in this directory.
#
# Before you apply this, create a 1Password service account for P0, with the
# permissions Read Items and Share Items on exactly the vaults people may
# request and no other vault, and store its token as the secret
# 1password/acme/token. The token starts with ops_. The example doesn't create
# the secret, which keeps the token out of Terraform's state. People can
# request items from every vault the service account can see. 1Password
# fixes a service account's vaults when it's created, so to change what's
# requestable later, create a new service account and store its token as a
# new version of the same secret.
#
# Creating p0_1password_account has the connector read the token, so the token
# must be in its secret by then. To store it, with the AWS CLI signed in to the
# secret's account, read the token without showing it:
#
#   read -rs OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN
#
# Then create the secret:
#
#   printf %s "$OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN" | aws secretsmanager create-secret \
#     --name 1password/acme/token \
#     --secret-string file:///dev/stdin --region us-west-2
#
# If the secret exists, store the token as a new version instead, which is also
# how to rotate it:
#
#   printf %s "$OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN" | aws secretsmanager put-secret-value \
#     --secret-id 1password/acme/token \
#     --secret-string file:///dev/stdin --region us-west-2

locals {
  p0_1password_account_acme = {
    # The connector's AWS account, which its role is in.
    connector_account_id = "123456789012"
    # The secret that holds the account's service account token: its name, and the
    # account and region it's in. P0 has the connector read the secret by this
    # name there. A new secret replaces the installation. To rotate the token,
    # add a new version to this secret instead.
    token_secret_name  = "1password/acme/token"
    secrets_account_id = "123456789012"
    secrets_region     = "us-west-2"
    # The ARN of the KMS key that encrypts the secret, if that's a
    # customer-managed key. The default aws/secretsmanager key needs nothing
    # for a secret in the connector's account, but can't be used from another
    # one. For a secret in another account, set this to its customer-managed
    # key, and in that account allow the connector's role
    # secretsmanager:GetSecretValue in the secret's resource policy and
    # kms:Decrypt through Secrets Manager in the key's policy.
    kms_key_arn = null
  }
}

# IAM is global, so the region only has to be one you use. Add the credential
# settings your other AWS providers use, such as profile or assume_role, if
# they have any.
provider "aws" {
  alias               = "p0_1password_account_acme"
  region              = local.p0_1password_account_acme.secrets_region
  allowed_account_ids = [local.p0_1password_account_acme.connector_account_id]
}

data "aws_partition" "p0_1password_account_acme" {
  provider = aws.p0_1password_account_acme
}

# The connector reads the account's service account token, and no other
# secret. The policy goes on the connector's role, which P0 names in
# connector_identity. Each 1Password account adds a policy of its own to that
# role, and a role's inline policies share a limit of 10,240 characters: past
# a few dozen accounts, deploy another connector for the rest.
resource "aws_iam_role_policy" "p0_1password_account_acme_token" {
  provider = aws.p0_1password_account_acme

  name = "Read1PasswordToken-acme.1password.com"
  role = p0_1password_connector.example.connector_identity.role_name
  policy = jsonencode({
    Version = "2012-10-17"
    Statement = concat(
      [{
        Sid    = "ReadAccessToken"
        Effect = "Allow"
        Action = "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue"
        # P0 gives the connector the secret's partial ARN: its ARN without the
        # hyphen and six random characters that end it. "??????" matches
        # those, so the connector gets this one secret and no other.
        Resource = join(":", [
          "arn:aws:secretsmanager",
          local.p0_1password_account_acme.secrets_region,
          local.p0_1password_account_acme.secrets_account_id,
          "secret",
          "${local.p0_1password_account_acme.token_secret_name}-??????",
        ])
      }],
      local.p0_1password_account_acme.kms_key_arn == null ? [] : [{
        Sid      = "DecryptAccessToken"
        Effect   = "Allow"
        Action   = "kms:Decrypt"
        Resource = local.p0_1password_account_acme.kms_key_arn
        Condition = {
          StringEquals = {
            "kms:ViaService" = "secretsmanager.${local.p0_1password_account_acme.secrets_region}.${data.aws_partition.p0_1password_account_acme.dns_suffix}"
          }
        }
      }],
    )
  })

  # A secret in another account can't use the default aws/secretsmanager key.
  lifecycle {
    precondition {
      condition     = local.p0_1password_account_acme.secrets_account_id == local.p0_1password_account_acme.connector_account_id || local.p0_1password_account_acme.kms_key_arn != null
      error_message = "The service account token's secret is in another AWS account, so it must be encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key. Set kms_key_arn to that key's ARN, and allow the connector's role in the secret's resource policy and in the key's policy."
    }
  }
}

# Adds the account. Creating it has P0 validate the install through the
# connector, so it waits until the connector can read the token. IAM changes
# can take a few seconds to take effect, so if the connector is denied the
# secret, apply again.
resource "p0_1password_account" "example" {
  id        = "acme.1password.com"
  connector = p0_1password_connector.example.id

  secret_manager = {
    type           = "aws-sm"
    account_id     = local.p0_1password_account_acme.secrets_account_id
    secrets_region = local.p0_1password_account_acme.secrets_region
  }
  token_secret_name = local.p0_1password_account_acme.token_secret_name

  # Each share link opens only once, so the person gets one look at the item
  # and should copy what they need. Unlike the fields above, this changes in
  # place, and applies to links made after the change. Off by default.
  one_time_links = true

  # How many open requests a person may have in this account: "user" for one
  # in the whole account, "vault" for one per vault, or "item" for one per
  # item. Changes in place. One per item by default.
  request_limit = "vault"

  depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy.p0_1password_account_acme_token]
}

# The email domains the connector shares items with, as P0 read them back from
# it.
output "onepassword_allowed_domains" {
  value = p0_1password_account.example.allowed_domains
}
```

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
## Schema

### Required

- `connector` (String) The connector that shares this account's items: the `id` of a `p0_1password_connector` resource. Requires that connector to be installed.
- `id` (String) The account's sign-in address, such as `acme.1password.com`: the host you sign in to 1Password at, in lowercase, ending in `.1password.com`, `.1password.ca` or `.1password.eu`.
- `secret_manager` (Attributes) The secret manager that holds the service account token. P0 never reads the token. Your connector does. It must be in the connector's cloud, and can be in another account or project. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedatt--secret_manager))
- `token_secret_name` (String) The name of the secret that holds the service account token, such as `1password/acme/token` in AWS Secrets Manager or `1password-acme-token` in Google Secret Manager: the name alone, not the secret's ARN or its full resource name. In AWS Secrets Manager the name can't end in a hyphen and six letters or digits, like `-AbCdEf`, because Secrets Manager can't find a secret by such a name. Changing it replaces the installation. To rotate the token, store the new one as a new version of the same secret, which needs no change here.

### Optional

- `one_time_links` (Boolean) Whether each share link opens only once. The person gets one look at the item, so they should copy what they need. Changing it applies to links made after the change, and updates the installation in place. Defaults to `false`.
- `request_limit` (String) How many open requests a person may have in this account: `user` for one in the whole account, `vault` for one per vault, or `item` for one per item. P0 refuses a request past the limit until the person revokes the open one. Changing it updates the installation in place. Defaults to `item`.

### Read-Only

- `allowed_domains` (String) The email domains the connector shares items with: the `DOMAIN_ALLOW_PATTERN` it's deployed with, which P0 reads back from the connector when it checks the install. To change it, change the connector's deployment.
- `state` (String) This item's install progress in the P0 application:
	- 'stage': The item has been staged for installation
	- 'configure': The item is available to be added to P0, and may be configured
	- 'installed': The item is fully installed

<a id="nestedatt--secret_manager"></a>
### Nested Schema for `secret_manager`

Required:

- `type` (String) The secret manager: either `aws-sm` (AWS Secrets Manager) or `gcp-sm` (Google Secret Manager)

Optional:

- `account_id` (String) The ID of the AWS account that holds the service account token's secret (in the P0 app, one of your AWS Secrets Manager installations). Required for, and only valid with, `aws-sm`.
- `project_id` (String) The ID of the Google Cloud project that holds the service account token's secret (in the P0 app, one of your Google Secret Manager installations). Required for, and only valid with, `gcp-sm`.
- `secrets_region` (String) The AWS region the service account token's secret is stored in, such as `us-west-2`. Required for, and only valid with, `aws-sm`.
